extracted.intended_audience: patent prosecutors (patent attorneys/agents) responding to U.S. 35 U.S.C. §103/KSR obviousness rejections
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for preparing written responses and arguments to overcome U.S. obviousness (§103) rejections under KSR and related MPEP/case-law standards. Covers required factual findings, common examiner rationales, secondary considerations, and defense strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham Factors
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) Determine the scope and content of the prior art; (2) Ascertain the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art; (3) Resolve the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; and (4) Consider objective indicia of non-obviousness (i.e., secondary considerations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this four-part analytical framework as the foundation for any obviousness analysis; factual findings on these points are required to support a prima facie conclusion of obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary Considerations / Objective Indicia
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of secondary considerations may include commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, copying by the industry, and unexpected results. They are a reality check on the first three Graham inquiries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all secondary considerations are equal; tie commercial success to the innovation (not to marketing/distribution). Long-felt but unresolved need is particularly strong. Secondary considerations must be considered with the other Graham factors and may be insufficient if the prima facie case of obviousness is very strong (see Pfizer v. Apotex, Leapfrog v. Fisher-Price).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nexus Requirement for Secondary Considerations (MPEP 716.01(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: To be given substantial weight, evidence of secondary considerations must be relevant to the claimed subject matter and there must be a factually and legally sufficient connection (nexus) between the evidence and the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must determine nexus and, if they find evidence insufficient to rebut prima facie obviousness, must specifically set forth facts and reasoning justifying that conclusion. Case examples: Hearing Components (nexus shown by licensing fee drop after expiration) and Muniauction (nexus lacking where evidence was not coextensive with claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherency limits in Obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery of a previously unappreciated property of prior art or a new use does not by itself render the old composition patentably new. Inherency may supply a missing limitation only under a high standard: the referenced material must necessarily present the limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facts are required to show the prior art necessarily presents the limitation (Par Pharmaceutical); an assumption without evidence is insufficient (Southwire); the mere possibility that a result may occur is not enough (In re Rijckaert); unknown properties cannot be deemed obvious (Honeywell, Metabolite). Key takeaways: (1) mere possibility insufficient; (2) require facts showing necessity; (3) avoid assumptions; (4) unknown cannot be obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: MPEP 2143 — KSR Rationales (overview)
rubrics_metrics.description: KSR rationales that the PTO commonly relies upon include: (1) combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results; (2) simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results; (3) use of known technique to improve similar devices; (4) applying a known technique to a known device ready for improvement; (5) 'obvious to try' — choosing from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions with a reasonable expectation of success; (6) known work in one field prompting predictable variations in same/different field; (7) some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art to combine references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rationales represent common grounds for §103 rejections under KSR; each rationale carries specific factual findings the examiner must articulate to support a rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: KSR Rationale — Combining Prior Art Elements (required findings)
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject based on combining prior art elements, Examiners must find (1) prior art included each claimed element (not necessarily in one reference); (2) one of ordinary skill could have combined the elements by known methods and each element in combination performs the same function as separately; (3) one of ordinary skill would have recognized the results of the combination were predictable; and (4) whatever additional Graham-based findings are necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proper rejection must resolve the Graham factual inquiries and articulate these findings — mere conclusory statements are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: KSR Rationale — Simple Substitution (required findings)
rubrics_metrics.description: For rejection by simple substitution, Examiners must find (1) a prior art device differing from the claimed device by substitution of components; (2) the substituted components/functions were known in the art; (3) one of ordinary skill could have substituted the known element and the results would have been predictable; and (4) any additional Graham-based findings necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner must supply reasoned analysis showing substitution was predictable; mere assertion of substitution without explanation fails to establish prima facie obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: KSR Rationale — Use of Known Technique to Improve Similar Devices (required findings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners must find (1) prior art contained a device; (2) there was a 'base' device upon which the claimed invention is an improvement; (3) there existed a 'comparable' device that had been improved in the same way; (4) one of ordinary skill could have applied that improvement technique to the base device with predictable results; and (5) any additional Graham-based findings necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show comparable device improvements and predictable application; identify the factual basis for why the improvement would be applied to the base device.

rubrics_metrics.name: KSR Rationale — Device 'Ready for Improvement' (required findings)
rubrics_metrics.description: To rely on this rationale, Examiners must find (1) a 'base' device in the prior art that the claimed invention improves; (2) a known technique applicable to that base device; (3) one of ordinary skill would have recognized applying the technique would yield predictable results and an improved system; and (4) any additional Graham-based findings necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must articulate why the base device was 'ready for improvement' and why application of the technique would have been predictable.

rubrics_metrics.name: KSR Rationale — 'Obvious to Try' (required findings)
rubrics_metrics.description: For 'obvious to try' rejections, Examiners must find (1) a recognized problem or need at the time of invention (may include design/market pressure); (2) a finite number of identified, predictable potential solutions; (3) one of ordinary skill could have pursued those solutions with a reasonable expectation of success; and (4) any additional Graham-based findings necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely showing knowledge of alternatives is insufficient; the examiner must show predictable solutions and reasonable expectation of success (see Abridged MPEP p.284).

rubrics_metrics.name: KSR Rationale — Known Work Inspiring Predictable Variations (required findings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners must find (1) prior art included a similar/analogous device in same or different field; (2) design incentives or market forces that would prompt adaptation; (3) differences were encompassed in known variations or principles in the prior art; (4) one of ordinary skill, in view of incentives, could have implemented the variation and it would have been predictable; and (5) any additional Graham-based findings necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate why the prior art would have suggested the specific variation and that the variation's results were predictable to one of ordinary skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: KSR Rationale — Teaching, Suggestion, or Motivation (TSM)
rubrics_metrics.description: One ground for combination is some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art that would have led one of ordinary skill to modify or combine references to arrive at the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While KSR diminished strict TSM formalism, some demonstrable reason to combine remains required; the examiner should articulate factual reasons (not merely conclusory statements) motivating combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: All Claim Limitations Must Be Accounted For
rubrics_metrics.description: If just one claim limitation is not accounted for by the examiner's rejection, the examiner has failed to present a prima facie case of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In responses, show any uncaptured limitation or that the examiner has not shown the missing limitation is present or would be supplied by common sense/inherency without evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching Away (defensive criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the prior art teaches away from combining certain known elements, discovery of a successful means of combining them is more likely to be nonobvious. Whether a reference teaches away is a question of fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Harris and other case law; distinguish mere disclosure of alternatives (which is not teaching away). Show affirmative teachings that would have discouraged the combination to rebut an obviousness rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for Rational Underpinnings / Reason to Combine
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be underlying evidence in the record constituting the 'rational underpinnings' for the reason to combine prior art elements in the manner asserted in the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR requires reasoned explanation — not just that a skilled artisan 'could' combine. Responses should point out absence of such rationale and demand factual support or offer counter-explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changing Principle of Operation (limits on trivial modification)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed modification that changes the principle of operation of a device or requires substantial reconstruction might still support obviousness if the Examiner identifies a persuasive reason why one of ordinary skill would have undertaken it; substantial modifications, however, are not mere substitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If modification changes operation or requires significant rebuilding, argue that the change is not a mere predictable substitution and that the examiner must provide strong factual support for obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defeating the Purpose of a Reference
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner's proposed modification cannot render a prior art reference unsatisfactory for its intended purpose; if the modification defeats the reference's purpose or makes it inoperable, that undermines the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Gordon and argue that the combination proposed by the examiner would make the reference unsuitable for its intended purpose, so it would not have been a candidate for the asserted modification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusive 'Obvious to Try' Assertions are Insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge alone is not a sufficient rationale to combine prior art teachings. An examiner's statement 'it's obvious to try' without evidence or explanation is inappropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Arendi and demand evidence showing finite predictable options and reasonable expectation of success; point out conclusory assertions and lack of record support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner-Created Problem (improper reasoning)
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection is improper if the examiner invents a problem in the primary reference solely in order to apply a secondary reference to solve that artificially created problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that the problem the examiner relies upon did not exist in the primary reference absent hindsight; demonstrate that the examiner's reasoning imposes a fact pattern not present in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sparse Technical Disclosure / No Speculation (rejection must rest on factual basis)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference relied upon must be sufficiently clear and explicit so skilled artisans can ascertain its meaning; examiners must supply requisite factual basis and may not resort to speculation, unfounded assumptions or hindsight reconstruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Turlay and In re Warner. Point out gaps where examiner's factual basis is missing and demand concrete evidence or explain why speculation invalidates the rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous Art Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: For a reference to be proper in an obviousness rejection, it must be analogous art: either (1) from the same field of endeavor, or (2) reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To show 'reasonably pertinent', the reference must logically have commended itself to an inventor addressing the problem (In re ICON). Examiner should explain why an inventor would have looked to the reference (In re Klein). If the applicant's specification shows a broader problem, restrictively viewing the problem to exclude references may be improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: No Per Se Rules — Fact-Specific Analysis Required
rubrics_metrics.description: Per se rules that eliminate the need for fact-specific analysis flout §103 and case law; reliance on per se rules of obviousness is legally incorrect and must cease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand claim-by-claim, fact-specific comparison to prior art; do not allow administrative convenience or board-sanctioned per se rules to substitute for required analysis (In re Ochiai).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of Success (must be shown for obviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness requires that a person of ordinary skill would have had a reasonable expectation of success in achieving the known goal; evidence showing no reasonable expectation of success may support nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the expectation-of-success analysis matches the actual claimed goal and not a different, less-challenging one (see Institut Pasteur v. Focarino).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contraindicated Modifications (physical capability vs. obviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical capability alone does not render something obvious if it is contraindicated; the proper inquiry is whether it would have been obvious to modify the prior art to arrive at the claimed function, not whether the prior art could perform the function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Giannelli: show that a modification was contraindicated and that examiner/board belief without evidence is insufficient to establish prima facie obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research Examiner/Art Unit–Specific Strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate how others have been successful with the specific examiner or art unit by searching PatentAdvisor's full-text IFW (Interview Form/Wrapper) documents to find effective arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examiner-specific data (percent of cases with 103 rejections, allowance rates with/without 103) and IFW examples to craft targeted, precedent-based responses tailored to the examiner's patterns.
